coach_says: Good, active move. f5 hits your bishop on e4 with tempo and gains space around your king, and it is as good as anything else here. Just keep an eye on the long diagonal: after Qc3 your knight on e5 is pinned to the king on h8, so a move like Qf6 to cover it comes next.

This is fine and still clearly winning. The knight on h7 is stuck: it is attacked by your bishop and rook, and it can't run because Nf8 or Nf6 drops material to your rooks, so Bd3 keeps it trapped. Simplest though was Bxh7+ straight away: when a piece is there to be taken for free, take it before giving the opponent a tempo like g4.

Good choice. Your bishop on d3 was attacked by the e4 pawn, and Ng4 gets your knight out of the way with tempo by hitting the rook on f6, so you have time to play Bxe4 next. Taking on e4 first is just as good.

In a rook endgame the most active rook usually decides it, and f4 hands that to Black: it kicks the rook off e5 to e4, from where it hits f4 and then swings to c4 to attack c2, tying your rook down to defence. Rd4 first was the move: your rook takes the fourth rank, attacks the loose pawn on b4 and keeps Black's rook out of e4 and c4. Before pushing pawns in a rook ending, ask which squares the push gives the enemy rook.

Bxd4 grabs a pawn, but the bishop on d4 is only protected by the knight on e2, and that knight is already attacked by Black's rook on c2. After Rxe2 Qxe2 Rxd4 you have given two minor pieces for a rook and a pawn, and Black's pieces take over. Before taking, check what defends your capturing piece and whether that defender can be removed; here the first job was to deal with the rook on your second rank, with Rc1 to challenge it.
